front: Describe the structure of a metal.
back: A regular lattice of positive ions, arranged in layers, surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons that move throughout the structure.
Electrons that do not belong to any one atom and are free to move throughout the structure.
Their delocalised electrons are free to move through the lattice and carry charge.

front: Why are metals good conductors of heat?
back: Fast-moving delocalised electrons carry thermal energy quickly through the metal.

front: Why are metals malleable and ductile?
back: Layers of positive ions slide over each other, and the sea of delocalised electrons keeps holding them together, so the metal changes shape without breaking.
Malleable: can be hammered or pressed into shape. Ductile: can be drawn into wires.

front: Why do most metals have high melting points?
back: The attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons is strong and acts throughout the lattice, so a lot of energy is needed to overcome it.

front: Why does a solid metal conduct electricity but a solid ionic compound does not?
back: The metal has delocalised electrons free to move; the ions in an ionic solid are fixed in place (they move only when molten or dissolved).

front: Which two properties make copper ideal for electrical wiring?
back: It is an excellent electrical conductor and it is ductile (can be drawn into wires).
